verses.1: Al-Mizan reads “Glorify the name of your Lord” (87:1) comprehensively: cleanse speech about God of every expression unworthy of His sanctity, incomparability, and transcendence. This tanzīh excludes invoking gods, partners, or intercessors beside Him; assigning them lordship or acts exclusive to God—creation, existentiation, provision, giving life, and causing death; and attributing to God defects such as weakness, ignorance, injustice, or negligence. Such verbal glorification accords with practical glorification and complete monotheism. “Your Lord” stresses that the One acknowledged as Lord must be named without anything contradicting the Lordship He has disclosed. Aʿlá, “the highest of the high who dominates everything,” modifies “your Lord,” not “name,” and supplies the reason for the command. The commentary prefers this inclusive reading over narrower exegetical proposals because it matches the chapter’s progression: the Prophet first purifies his speech of explicit and implicit polytheism, is promised recitation without forgetting, has the path of preaching eased, and is then commanded to admonish.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says these verses prove the Lordship of the Lord named in (87:1). Khalq is assembling a thing's parts, and taswiyah is proportioning and placing every constituent where it belongs, as organs in a body. Despite their unqualified wording, both apply only to aspects of creation that are composite in some respect.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says God measures creation through precise limits that pervade creatures' being, attributes, and functions, then supplies faculties suited to their ordained functions and perfections. This is guidance: every creature pursues what its Lord has determined for it. The commentary illustrates that order through (15:21), (80:20), and (2:148).
verses.4: Al-Mizan defines al-marʿā as what animals graze on, which God brings forth by making plants grow. Ghuthāʾ is flood-deposited vegetation and twigs, or, according to some exegetes, withered plants; aḥwā means black. Bringing pasture forth and turning it to black scum are both instances of God's lordly direction of affairs, like His creating, proportioning, measuring, and guiding.

verses.6: Al-Mizan explains qirāʾah as combining letters and words in recitation; al-Mufradāt excludes both a single letter and every ordinary gathering. It reports Majmaʿ al-bayān's sense of iqrāʾ as listening to a reciter to correct slips, but says that is not meant here: there is no record that the Prophet recited the Qur'an wrongly, forgot revelation, or then corrected it. Rather, God promises to fortify him to retain and recite revelation exactly as revealed, without addition, omission, or distortion through forgetfulness, ensuring its delivery. The exception in (87:7) does not exclude particular forgotten portions; that would be a universal human condition, not a favor. It preserves God's absolute power to make the Prophet forget, although He does not will it, like the exception in (11:108). The commentary also relates the promise to the Prophet's fear of forgetting while Gabriel was still imparting revelation, and argues a sequence with (75:16-19) and (20:114). God's knowledge of al-jahr, what is manifest and readily perceptible, and what is hidden justifies His care for the Prophet's inward concern and obedience. The shift from ‘We’ to ‘Allah’ substantiates that this gift neither limits divine omnipotence nor knowledge.

verses.8: Al-Mizan calls taysīr the same as tashīl and understands the promise as God's preparing the Prophet for the smoothest verbal and practical path in conveying the message: guiding some, completing the argument against others, and enduring their harassment. The unusual wording, rather than ‘make the easier easy for you,’ focuses on fortifying his soul for the mission. It means rooting him firmly in fiṭrah, for the easiest path is that of fiṭrah; an author's note explains lil-yusrā as the elided ‘easier way,’ and the commentary compares this to (7:105).
verses.9: Al-Mizan treats the faʾ as the conclusion of the prior preparation for preaching: after the command to glorify God, the guarantee of unfailing recitation, and the easing of the Prophet's path, he is to admonish where admonition benefits. The condition is real, since God does not command a futile act. He must initially and repeatedly admonish those who fear God, whose hearts can benefit; initially admonish the wretched without fear to complete the proof against them; and not repeat admonition where it no longer benefits, as in (53:29). The commentary rejects readings that make in mean qad or idh and claim admonition always helps, citing (2:6-7); it also rejects an implied command to admonish whether useful or not, and a regretful condition, since the next verse confirms that those who fear do benefit.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says that anyone with fear of God and His punishment in the heart is awakened and admonished by the Qur'an.
verses.11: Al-Mizan identifies the pronoun with the admonition of (87:9): the most wretched, having no fear of God, turn away from it. Tajannub means distancing oneself, like tabāʿud. The greatest fire apparently is hellfire, greater than worldly fires, though some take it as hell's lowest and most intense levels. Thumma marks a new part of the statement, not a temporal interval: neither living nor dying there means no deliverance, neither death ending pain nor a change from wretched, tormented existence into happy, comfortable life.

verses.14: Al-Mizan defines tazakkī as self-purification and applies it to purification from worldly attachments, return to God, spending in His way to purge financial attachment, and wuḍūʾ as symbolic purification before prayer. It takes remembering the Lord as verbal invocation and prayer as the specific daily ritual. Though the wording is general, it reports narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt, alongside Sunni narrations, that apply these verses to zakāt and the Eid al-Fiṭr prayer.

verses.16: Al-Mizan defines īthār as choosing or preferring and reads the address as a rebuke to people generally for their tendency to attach themselves to worldly life and its improvement, though some restrict it to disbelievers. The shift to the second person heightens that rebuke. The hereafter is everlasting, but the comparative context states sufficiently that it is better and more lasting than this life and should therefore be preferred.

verses.18: Al-Mizan takes ‘This’ to refer to the preceding four verses (87:14-17), though some restrict it to the statement that the hereafter is better and more lasting. The initially unspecified former scriptures are then identified as those of Abraham and Moses; the presentation conveys their marked veneration and glorification.
